tldr: By adapting the inputs and outputs of a robot-arm world action model (WAM) to a quadruped and pairing on-policy self-distillation with task-specific reinforcement learning, this work speeds up inference by 14x while achieving an 85.0% success rate on language-conditioned quadrupedal loco-manipulation.
hero_caption: Pipeline for Stage 1: Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration. The vision and action interfaces of an arm-centric world action model are swapped and fine-tuned for a quadruped robot, then distilled via on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) into a fast student model that runs in just a few steps.
overview:
Arm-free quadrupedal loco-manipulation—standing on three legs while manipulating objects with a front leg—is an appealing approach because it handles varied tasks with a lightweight, simple mechanism. However, no general policy existed that could follow natural language instructions to manipulate objects with a foot, and collecting demonstration data was very difficult. Meanwhile, world action models (WAMs), which predict future observations and actions simultaneously, have shown high generalization performance. Still, existing WAMs are built for stationary robot arms and rely on long diffusion denoising loops, making them far too slow for real-time control.

To solve this, the authors proposed WAM-Policy, a two-stage framework that adapts and accelerates a pretrained arm WAM for quadruped robots. In the first stage, only the vision and action interfaces are swapped for quadruped counterparts, adapting the model with limited data. Then, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD)—learning directly from the teacher's generation process—dramatically slashes inference steps down to 1 video step and 2 action steps, achieving a 14x speedup. In the second stage, to break through the limits of imitation learning, the authors train task-specific expert teachers on challenging tasks via reinforcement learning, merging these slow specialists into a single fast student through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD).

For evaluation, the team built QLM-Bench, a simulation benchmark consisting of 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation. In experiments, the accelerated student model preserved a 76.7% success rate, well above the un-distilled few-step baseline (69.3%). After reinforcement learning and policy merging, performance reached 85.0%, surpassing even the original slow teacher (77.0%). Finally, the authors demonstrated that a policy trained purely in simulation could be zero-shot deployed onto a real Unitree Go2 Air.
contributions: Established a cross-morphology policy adaptation method that transfers an arm-pretrained world action model to foot loco-manipulation simply by replacing its input and output interfaces.

Accelerated inference by 14x (1 video step and 2 action steps) without sacrificing performance using on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), which regresses the student onto teacher trajectories generated from the exact same noise.

Broke through the ceiling of imitation learning by enhancing slow specialist teachers with task-specific reinforcement learning and merging them into one fast student via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD).
Built and released QLM-Bench, a new benchmark featuring 1,000 multimodal demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, and proved real-world viability on a physical Unitree Go2 Air.

sections.heading: Bringing World Action Models to Arm-Free Quadruped Robots
sections.summary: Arm-free quadrupeds manipulating objects with a front leg are lightweight and navigate rough terrain well, but lacked an end-to-end policy that follows language instructions. This paper brings a powerful world action model (WAM) to quadrupeds, tackling the two hurdles of slow computation and imitation learning limits.
sections.details:
Quadruped robots can traverse rough terrain where wheeled or fixed-base robots cannot go. Using a front leg as an end-effector for loco-manipulation without mounting an extra arm is an ideal approach that avoids added weight and mechanical complexity. However, existing vision-based foot manipulation methods rely on point clouds, and no end-to-end system existed that could follow natural language instructions.

Recently, world action models (WAMs) that predict future scenes and actions by leveraging visual pretraining priors have achieved strong results in manipulation. This work sets out to bring WAMs to arm-free quadruped robots. However, two major hurdles stand in the way.

The first is the gap in morphology and slow inference. Existing WAMs (such as LingBot-VA, the foundation used here) assume robot arms, outputting 30-dimensional bimanual commands from head and wrist cameras. A quadruped, on the other hand, has cameras fixed to its body that shake heavily during movement, and its manipulating leg must also support its body weight. Furthermore, because WAMs sample iteratively over many network function evaluations (NFEs), generating 0.32 seconds of robot motion takes 2.226 seconds, making real-time control impossible.

The second is the limit of imitation learning. Even if distillation accelerates the model, it cannot outperform human or synthesized demonstrations as long as the original teacher is trained purely via imitation. Reinforcement learning with task-specific rewards can overcome this limitation, but it produces separate, slow specialist models for each task that need to be unified into a single fast policy.

WAM-Policy tackles these issues through a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 handles cross-morphology adaptation and self-distillation, and Stage 2 covers task-specific reinforcement learning and policy merging.

sections.heading: Loco-Manipulation, World Action Models, and Policy Distillation
sections.summary: This section reviews four technical domains: language-conditioned quadruped control, world action models, few-step distillation, and RL policy merging. This work is the first to apply a WAM to foot-based manipulation on an arm-free quadruped.
sections.details:
### Quadruped Loco-Manipulation
Traditional language-guided quadrupeds mostly combine Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with low-level controllers for walking speed or navigation. When manipulation is needed, systems typically mount an arm or gripper, or rely on point-cloud-based RL/imitation learning (such as Leg-Manip). No unified policy directly controlled foot manipulation from language instructions and RGB images.

### World Action Models (WAMs)
WAMs predict future scenes and actions simultaneously using video generative models as backbones, primarily studied on stationary arms or humanoids. Existing quadruped world models have focused purely on locomotion and navigation; none addressed foot manipulation while supporting body weight. This work introduces a new direction by transferring an existing arm WAM to an entirely different robot morphology.

### Few-Step WAMs and On-Policy Distillation
Distillation is essential to speed up diffusion and flow-matching models that require iterative denoising loops. While offline distillation methods exist, closed-loop control suffers from environment-level exposure bias as errors from the student's own actions accumulate. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) introduces a novel twist: the student's on-policy rollouts in closed loop are supervised directly by the same model running with a higher computational budget (the teacher).

### Reinforcement Learning and Policy Merging
Applying reinforcement learning to diffusion or flow models effectively breaks through the imitation ceiling, but per-task optimization causes specialist models to proliferate. While prior work like Multi-Teacher OPD merged policies without reducing sampling steps, M-OPD in this work consolidates multiple slow specialist teachers into a single student that runs in just 1 video step and 2 action steps.

sections.heading: The Two-Stage Architecture of WAM-Policy: Adapt, Accelerate, Improve, and Merge
sections.summary: Stage 1 replaces input/output interfaces for quadrupeds, fine-tunes the model, and slashes inference steps via on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). Stage 2 builds expert teachers using task-specific RL and merges them into a single fast student through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD).
sections.details:
### 3.1 Stage 1: Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration
The base model uses LingBot-VA, initialized from the Wan2.2-5B video generator. Given context $H_k$ (instruction, latent representations of past RGB observations, and past actions), the video stream predicts a latent plan $Z_k$ for future observations, while the action stream acts as an inverse dynamics model to estimate the action chunk $A_k$.

- **Vision and Action Adaptation (Stage 1.1)**: The arm head/wrist cameras are replaced with a wide-angle forward-facing ego view and a top-down view looking down at the workspace. The action space is swapped for a 9-dimensional command (base planar velocity, yaw velocity, foot target position, and target contact force) fed into a whole-body controller (RAMBO) managing three-legged walking and front-leg manipulation. Only the input/output projection layers are reinitialized, followed by flow-matching training on quadruped demonstration data.
- **On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD, Stage 1.2)**: Because generating one chunk (0.32 seconds) takes 2.226 seconds with the transferred model, this model serves as teacher $\pi_{\mathrm{T}}$ and is distilled into student $\pi_{\mathrm{S}}$ equipped with LoRA parameters $\Delta$. The student's compute is fixed to 1 video step and 2 action steps (1/2-NFE). Latent plans and action chunks generated by the teacher from the exact same initial noise serve as targets, regressed via a pseudo-Huber loss. Training data mixes 50% teacher-cached trajectories with 50% student online rollouts, allowing the student to recover from its own drift.

### 3.2 Stage 2: Task-Specific Improvement and Merging
The imitation-based OPSD student hits a performance plateau bounded by the teacher (77.0% success rate).

- **Task-Specific RL (Stage 2.1)**: On two failure-prone tasks (box pushing and door opening), expert teachers are trained using DiffusionNFT, an RL method based on flow-matching losses. Rolling out multiple windows from the same starting state with different noise seeds, the policy is updated based on rewards derived from object movement distance and foot contact.
- **Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (M-OPD, Stage 2.2)**: An ensemble teacher $\pi_{\mathrm{M}}$ routes queries to the corresponding expert teacher (for improved tasks) or the original teacher (for the other 8 tasks) based on the instruction. Starting from the OPSD student, the model rolls out online and regresses to the ensemble teacher's outputs, yielding a single, versatile student capable of running all tasks at 1/2-NFE.

captions.F3: Top: Flow of on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). Given context mixing teacher caches and student online rollouts, the student mimics high-precision teacher outputs generated from identical noise. Bottom: Conceptual diagram of task-specific RL and multi-teacher distillation (M-OPD) in Stage 2.

sections.heading: QLM-Bench: A Benchmark with 1,000 Demonstrations Synthesized Without Teleoperation
sections.summary: The authors created QLM-Bench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating language-conditioned quadrupedal loco-manipulation. High-quality demonstration data totaling 1,000 episodes was generated via large multimodal models without manual teleoperation.
sections.details:
### Benchmark Environment and Task Setup
QLM-Bench is a MuJoCo-based benchmark where a Unitree Go2 manipulates diverse objects using its front-left leg. It contains 10 tasks:

1. Close the refrigerator door
2. Close the oven door
3. Turn the valve
4. Pull the drawer open
5. Press the room door handle to open it
6. Press the button
7. Lift the basket
8. Kick the ball into the goal
9. Push the box into the target area
10. Sweep the block into the target area

Each task features a forward-facing ego camera, a top-down camera looking down at the feet, and a 9-dimensional low-level control command.

### Teleoperation-Free Data Synthesis Pipeline
Because quadruped foot manipulation involves high degrees of freedom coupled with balance control, gathering demonstrations via manual teleoperation is exceptionally difficult. In this work, a large multimodal model (OpenAI Codex) was prompted with concise task descriptions to generate rough reference command trajectories. After visual verification by a human, these trajectories were executed by the whole-body controller while randomizing scene layouts, saving only successful episodes. This pipeline efficiently collected 100 demonstrations per task—1,000 multimodal demonstrations in total (two camera views, executed commands, and language instructions)—without any direct human teleoperation.

captions.F4: The 10 tasks included in QLM-Bench. They span varied, challenging loco-manipulation behaviors, from delicate lever pressing with the foot to walking while closing doors, pushing boxes, and kicking balls.

sections.heading: Sim and Real Validations: 14x Speedup and 85% Success Rate
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across all 10 tasks in QLM-Bench. OPSD achieved a 14x inference speedup while preserving a 76.7% success rate, and Stage 2 RL with M-OPD lifted success to 85.0%. Real-world deployment on a Go2 Air was also verified.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Evaluation Protocol and Baselines
Evaluations used the Standard100 protocol on QLM-Bench (10 unseen scene layouts $\times$ 3 policy seeds per task, totaling 300 episodes). Baselines included an un-distilled student (running identical weights at 1/2-NFE) and a reproduced point-cloud baseline, Leg-Manip.

### 5.2 Stage 1 Results: Adaptation and Acceleration
- **Cross-Morphology Transfer**: The high-NFE teacher transferred from the arm WAM achieved an average success rate of 77.0% across all 10 tasks, substantially outperforming Leg-Manip (61.7%), which trains separate point-cloud planners per task.
- **Inference Speed and Distillation**: The original teacher required 2.226 seconds per chunk (roughly 7x slower than real time). Simply evaluating it at 1/2-NFE caused failures on tasks like drawer opening and valve turning, dropping success to 69.3%. In contrast, the OPSD-trained student cut inference time to 0.156–0.159 seconds (**a 14x speedup**) while fully recovering a **76.7%** success rate, matching the teacher.

### 5.3 Stage 2 Results: Reinforcement Learning and Multi-Teacher Merging
On tasks where the teacher struggled—box pushing (47%) and door opening (53%)—the Stage 2.1 RL expert teachers reached 100% success. The consolidated 1/2-NFE student from Stage 2.2 M-OPD achieved 90% on box pushing and 87% on door opening, raising the overall 10-task average to **85.0%**. This surpasses the original high-NFE teacher (77.0%) by 8 percentage points.

### 5.4 Key Ablation Findings
- **Training Context Source**: Comparing teacher cache only, student streaming only, and a 50/50 mix yielded similar success rates between 76.3% and 77.0%. Regressing on identical-noise teacher outputs proved to be the core driver of performance.
- **Adding Proprioception**: Adding a 10-dimensional state vector (robot velocity, orientation, etc.) to inputs and predictions to compensate for body sway actually decreased the success rate to 67%. Operating purely on RGB images proved superior to enforcing state prediction.

### 5.5 Real-Robot Deployment
The simulation-trained OPSD student was deployed on a physical Unitree Go2 Air equipped with an external RealSense D435i and its onboard camera. Across 30 trials over three tasks (button pressing, ball kicking, and box pushing), the policy achieved 7 successful runs without any real-world fine-tuning.

captions.F5: Comparison of rollouts on the physical Unitree Go2 Air (top) and the simulation environment (bottom). Real-world trials reproduce the same foot manipulation behaviors seen in simulation across button pressing, ball kicking, and box pushing.
captions.F6: Hardware configuration of the physical Unitree Go2 Air. Video streams from the internal camera (ego) and top-mounted RealSense (top-down) are sent to a PC, where WAM-Policy outputs commands converted to joint torques by the whole-body controller RAMBO.

sections.heading: Summary and What Lies Ahead
sections.summary: WAM-Policy successfully adapts, accelerates, and improves an arm world action model for language-driven quadruped foot manipulation. Its effectiveness was demonstrated in both simulation and real-world experiments.
sections.details:
This work presented WAM-Policy, a framework that converts a pretrained arm world action model into a language-conditioned loco-manipulation policy for quadruped robots.

Stage 1 accelerates inference by 14x through cross-morphology adaptation and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). Stage 2 overcomes imitation learning limits via task-specific RL and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD), ultimately achieving an 85.0% success rate at a fraction of the computational cost. In addition, the team built QLM-Bench with 1,000 synthesized demonstrations and validated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical robot.

Future work includes generalizing RL reward designs beyond box pushing and door opening, evaluating generalization on unseen tasks and alternative robot morphologies, and reducing the real-robot observation encoding latency (currently 0.66 seconds) below 0.32 seconds for strict real-time control.

takeaways: A large world action model (WAM) pretrained on robot arms can successfully transfer to an entirely different morphology—quadrupedal foot manipulation—simply by swapping its vision and action projection layers.
Even with slow flow-matching WAMs, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) regressing onto teacher trajectories from identical noise compresses sampling to 1/2-NFE (14x faster) without losing accuracy.

When imitation learning plateaus, training slow expert teachers via task-specific RL and consolidating them through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD) lets a single few-step student break the teacher's performance ceiling.

Even for complex dynamics like quadruped manipulation, pairing multimodal LLM trajectory generation with physics-based success filtering enables automatic synthesis of 1,000 high-quality demonstrations without human teleoperation.
limitations: Closed-loop latency bottleneck on real hardware: While model inference is fast at 0.159 seconds, image VAE encoding and processing push total step latency to 0.66 seconds, exceeding the 0.32-second chunk duration and falling short of strict real-time control.

Reward engineering cost for RL: Stage 2 reinforcement learning was applied to only two tasks (box pushing and door opening), requiring manually designed, object-trajectory-based reward functions for each task.

Sim-to-real performance gap: Because deployment is strictly zero-shot without real-world data, the physical success rate (7 out of 30 trials) remains substantially lower than the simulation performance (over 80%).
